grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Grande quantidade:**
- **a lot of / lots of** + contável e incontável (principalmente afirmativas): a lot of money, lots of bills
- **many** + contável · **much** + incontável → principalmente em **perguntas e negativas**: How much debt? / not many options
- **plenty of** = mais que suficiente: "Don't worry, we have **plenty of** time."

**Pequena quantidade — a diferença sutil:**
- **a few** (contável) / **a little** (incontável) = **alguns, um pouco** → sentido **positivo** (é suficiente)
  "I have **a little** money saved. Let's go out!"
- **few** / **little** (sem "a") = **poucos, pouco** → sentido **negativo** (quase nada)
  "**Few** people save enough for retirement." / "There's **little** hope."

**Excesso e falta:**
- **too much** + incontável / **too many** + contável = demais (problema): "I spend **too much** money on apps." / "I have **too many** subscriptions."
- **(not) enough** + substantivo = (não) suficiente: "I don't have **enough** savings."

**Nenhum:**
- **no** + substantivo = "There's **no** money left." (= not any)
- **none (of)** sozinho: "How much is left? **None**."

examples.en: Few Brazilians have an emergency fund, but a few apps are trying to change that.
examples.pt: Poucos brasileiros têm reserva de emergência, mas alguns apps estão tentando mudar isso.

examples.en: I had too many subscriptions, so I cancelled a few of them.
examples.pt: Eu tinha assinaturas demais, então cancelei algumas.

examples.en: We don't have much time, but we have plenty of ideas.

grammar.tip_pt: **Money** é incontável, mas **reais / dollars / coins / bills** são contáveis: "How **much money**?" x "How **many dollars**?"

listening.title: Financial tips podcast
listening.context_pt: Um educador financeiro dá dicas em um podcast.

lines.speaker: Educator
lines.en: Here are a few rules I teach everyone. One: before you buy something that isn't essential, wait 48 hours. Most impulse purchases don't survive the wait. Two: try the 50-30-20 rule — 50% of your income for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings or paying debt. Three: build an emergency fund. Ideally, you should have enough to cover three to six months of expenses. And four: be careful with credit card debt. In some countries, the interest rates are extremely high — few loans are more expensive. If you can't pay the full bill, cut back on something else before you pay only the minimum.

reading.title: Cashless societies
reading.text: In just a few years, the way people pay for things has changed dramatically. In Sweden, very few shops still accept cash, and some banks no longer handle coins and notes at all. In Brazil, Pix — the instant payment system launched by the Central Bank in 2020 — became one of the most widely used payment methods in the country in a remarkably short time. Street vendors, taxi drivers and even beggars now display QR codes. The advantages are clear: payments are fast, free for individuals and convenient. But there are concerns too. Digital payments make it easier to spend without noticing — paying with a phone doesn't "hurt" as much as handing over a banknote. Fraud and scams have also increased. And not everyone has a smartphone or a bank account, so a fully cashless society could leave the most vulnerable people behind. The question is not whether cash will disappear, but how quickly — and who will pay the price.

questions.answer: Very few shops accept cash and some banks don't handle coins and notes.

questions.q: Who could be left behind in a cashless society?
questions.answer: People without a smartphone or bank account (the most vulnerable).

writing.model:
5 money tips for young people

1. Track every expense for a month. Most people are surprised by how much money they spend on small things like snacks and apps.
2. Cancel what you don't use. Many of us have too many subscriptions — a few of them we haven't opened in months.
3. Be careful with installments. Paying in ten installments feels easy, but if you have too many, there will be little money left at the end of the month.
4. Start an emergency fund, even with a little money. Few students can save a lot, but saving something every month builds a powerful habit.
5. Learn the basics of investing. You don't need much money to start, and there are plenty of free courses online.

Remember: financial freedom isn't about earning a lot. It's about spending less than you earn — and making sure you always have enough for the unexpected.

grammar.title: Present perfect x past simple (nível B1+)
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já conhece a regra básica (tempo terminado x aberto). No B1+, veja como os dois tempos **trabalham juntos** em textos de não ficção e notícias:

**1. Present perfect para apresentar o tema ou resultado atual → past simple para os detalhes:**
"Scientists **have studied** self-control for decades. The first famous experiment **took place** at Stanford in the 1960s."

**2. Present perfect com `since` + past simple na outra parte:**
"**Since** the study **was published**, many researchers **have tried** to replicate it."

**3. Superlativo + present perfect (ever):**
"It's **the most famous** psychology experiment I**'ve ever read** about."

**4. `It's the first time` + present perfect:**
"**It's the first time** I**'ve saved** money for a whole year."

**5. Expressões de período aberto (present perfect):** recently, lately, so far, up to now, over the past few years, in the last decade
"**Over the past few years**, researchers **have questioned** the original conclusions."

**Expressões de tempo fechado (past simple):** in the 1960s, at that time, back then, when I was..., years ago, at first
"**At that time**, nobody **questioned** the results."

rows: Scientists have studied it for 50 years.
The first study took place in 1968.
Over the past decade, many people have questioned it.
In 2018, a new study was published.
Yesterday I ate a whole box.

listening.title: Willpower and phones
listening.context_pt: Uma neurocientista fala sobre autocontrole na era dos smartphones.

lines.speaker: Scientist
lines.en: Over the past fifteen years, our relationship with temptation has changed completely. In the 1960s, the temptation in the experiment was a marshmallow on a table. Today, it's in our pocket all day: notifications, videos, online shopping. Apps have been designed by very smart people to capture our attention. So if you've ever felt that you have no willpower, it's not entirely your fault. The best strategy isn't to fight harder — it's to change your environment. In one study, people who simply put their phones in another room performed better on memory tests. Out of sight, out of mind.

reading.title: What the marshmallow test really tells us
reading.text: The marshmallow test is one of the most famous experiments in psychology. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, researchers at Stanford University offered preschool children a choice: eat one treat now, or wait alone for about fifteen minutes and get two. Years later, follow-up studies suggested that the children who had waited tended to have better school results and other positive outcomes. The idea spread quickly: self-control, it seemed, was a key to success. Since then, however, the story has become more complicated. The original groups were small and mostly came from families connected to the university. In 2018, a larger study with a more diverse group of children found a much weaker connection, and much of it seemed to be explained by factors like family income and education. Other researchers have shown that children wait longer when they trust the adult who made the promise. So the test may measure not only willpower, but also experience: if promises in your life have often been broken, eating the marshmallow now is a rational choice.

questions.q: What was the problem with the original groups?
questions.answer: They were small and mostly from families connected to the university.

questions.q: Why might eating the marshmallow now be a rational choice?

writing.model:
The marshmallow test has become one of the best-known experiments in psychology. In the 1960s and 70s, researchers at Stanford gave young children a choice between one treat now and two later, and follow-up studies suggested that the children who waited did better in life. However, since then, larger studies have found that family background explains much of this difference, and that trust also affects how long children wait.

In my opinion, self-control is important, but it isn't the whole story. I've always been quite disciplined, but I know that discipline is easier when you have stability. When I was a child, my parents always kept their promises, so waiting felt safe. Many children don't have that experience. So instead of telling people to "just be more disciplined", I think we should also create environments where waiting is worth it — like fair schools, stable jobs and trustworthy institutions.

grammar.title: Present perfect simple x continuous
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)** → foco no **processo**, na **duração**, na **atividade** (que pode ainda não ter terminado):
- "I**'ve been writing** my thesis **for** two years." (processo em andamento)
- "She**'s been training** every day." (esforço repetido)
- "Why are you so tired? — I**'ve been studying** all night." (atividade recente com efeito visível)

**Present perfect simple (have + particípio)** → foco no **resultado**, na **quantidade**, no que foi **concluído**:
- "I**'ve written** three chapters." (quantidade concluída)
- "She**'s won** two medals."
- "I**'ve finished** my thesis!" (completo)

**Pergunta-chave:**
- **How long** have you been...? → duração (continuous)
- **How many / How much** have you...? → quantidade (simple)

**Stative verbs** (know, believe, have [posse], want, own) → sempre simple: "I**'ve known** her for years."

**Live, work, study, teach** → com for/since, os dois são possíveis com pouca diferença; o continuous sugere algo mais **temporário**: "I've lived here all my life" (permanente) x "I've been living here since March" (temporário).

reading.title: The myth of talent
reading.text: When we see a brilliant musician, athlete or entrepreneur, we often assume they were simply born with a special talent. But researchers who study expertise tell a different story. In a famous study in the 1990s, psychologist Anders Ericsson looked at violin students at a music academy in Berlin. He found that the best students had practiced significantly more hours than the others — and, crucially, that they had practiced in a specific way. Ericsson called it "deliberate practice": working on your weaknesses, getting regular feedback and constantly pushing beyond your comfort zone. Writer Malcolm Gladwell later popularized the idea as the "10,000-hour rule", although Ericsson himself said that the number was not a magic rule. Since then, other scientists have argued that factors like genes, starting age and opportunity also matter. Still, the main lesson remains: behind most "overnight successes" there are years of invisible, focused work.

grammar.title: Should have / shouldn't have + particípio
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Should have + particípio** → algo que **deveria ter acontecido, mas não aconteceu** (arrependimento ou crítica sobre o passado):
- "I **should have checked** the numbers." (não conferi — me arrependo)
- "You **should have told** me earlier!" (você não me contou — crítica)

**Shouldn't have + particípio** → algo que **aconteceu, mas não deveria**:
- "I **shouldn't have sent** that email." (mandei — erro)
- "You **shouldn't have spent** so much money!" (às vezes é carinho, ao receber um presente!)

Na fala: **should have** = "**shúdav**" ou até "**shúda**".

**Estrutura de um bom pedido de desculpas profissional:**
1. **Reconheça:** "I'm sorry for / I apologize for + -ing / substantivo": "I apologize for **missing** the deadline."
2. **Assuma a responsabilidade** (sem culpar outros): "It was my fault. I **should have** asked for help earlier."
3. **Explique** brevemente (sem desculpas longas): "I underestimated how long it would take."
4. **Ofereça solução:** "I'll send it by 10 tomorrow."
5. **Prevenção:** "In future, I'll make sure to..."

⚠️ **Sorry for** + -ing/substantivo (sobre algo que você fez) · **sorry to** + verbo (algo que você está fazendo agora): "Sorry **to bother** you." / "Sorry **for being** late."

grammar.tip_pt: O famoso **"I did my best"** (fiz o meu melhor) pode soar como desculpa se vier sozinho. Combine com responsabilidade e solução: "I did my best, but I should have asked for help sooner. Here's what I'll do now..."

reading.title: The anatomy of a good apology
reading.text: Why do some apologies make things better while others make them worse? Researchers who study communication have identified several elements that make an apology effective. The most important one, according to some studies, is acknowledging responsibility: saying clearly "It was my fault" or "I made a mistake". The second is offering to repair the damage. Expressing regret ("I'm sorry") matters too, but on its own it often isn't enough. Interestingly, long explanations can backfire: if you spend too much time explaining why something happened, people may hear it as an excuse. The worst apologies are "non-apologies" — phrases like "I'm sorry if you were offended" or "Mistakes were made", which avoid taking real responsibility. Public figures and companies use them all the time, and audiences usually notice. The lesson? A good apology is short, specific and focused on the other person, not on yourself.

questions.answer: Acknowledging responsibility.

questions.q: Why can long explanations backfire?
questions.answer: People may hear them as excuses.

questions.q: What is a "non-apology"?
questions.answer: A phrase that avoids taking real responsibility (e.g., "I'm sorry if you were offended").

questions.q: How should a good apology be?
questions.answer: Short, specific and focused on the other person.
